entries.text: Can you access work I did on a different computer in VSCode?
entries.reply:
Yes, but only for work you've pushed to GitHub. This session runs in a cloud container with a fresh clone of `mraottth/projects`. Your other computer's disk isn't reachable from here, so uncommitted or unpushed changes in VS Code are invisible to me.

**What I can see:** I fetched every branch, and your pushes through yesterday (2026-09-27) are all here and merged into `main`. That's the Shelf Life / book recommender work:
- Demo library, homepage choices and the cover-flow transition (`br-demo-and-transition`)
- The repo reorganization (`br-portfolio-order`)
- Prediction calibration (Goodreads-shrunk means) and the fame-gated ranking boost
- The Assistant tab / chatbot (`br-chatbot`)
- The Cloud Run deploy

If you did anything after those commits, or never pushed it, I can't see it.

**To get newer work to me:** on the other computer, run this in the VS Code terminal:
```
git add -A
git commit -m "WIP"
git push
```
You can also use the Source Control panel: commit, then Sync/Push. Tell me the branch name afterwards and I'll pull it.

Which work did you have in mind? I can check whether it's among what's already here.

entries.text: great, can you update min-instances to 1 for me on my cloud run of Shelf Life?
entries.reply:
I couldn't change the live Cloud Run service because this cloud session has no `gcloud` and no Google Cloud credentials. Instead, I updated your deploy settings so `make deploy` now sets min-instances to 1 instead of resetting it to 0. That change is pushed to the `claude/vscode-cross-computer-access-bf9nn6` branch.

**To change the live service now**, run this on your computer. It only changes the setting and doesn't rebuild the app:
```
gcloud run services update goodrec --project v2-book-recommender --region us-central1 --min-instances 1
```

**What I changed in the repo:**
- In `Makefile`, the deploy command now uses `--min-instances 1` instead of `0`, and I updated the comment next to it.
- In `CLAUDE.md`, the note that said "scale to zero" now says "min 1 warm instance".

If you merge that branch into `main`, future deploys will keep the setting.

Keeping one instance running all the time costs money even when nobody is using the app. Scaling to zero was free when idle. With 1 CPU and 1 GiB memory, one always-on instance costs very roughly $10–15 a month with Cloud Run's lower idle pricing. It will be noticeably more if CPU is set to be always allocated. Check the Cloud Run pricing page for exact numbers.

entries.text: when a new user goes to the site for the first time and nobody has been on the site in a long time, what should they expect the load time to be with min instances at 0 and at 1?
entries.reply:
I can't give you measured numbers from here. The model files aren't in the repo and I can't reach your Cloud Run logs. Based on what the app does when it starts, here are my estimates for a visitor arriving after the site has been idle:

| | min-instances 0 | min-instances 1 |
|---|---|---|
| Wait before anything appears | **about 5–15 s**, probably around 8–10 s | **under 1 s** |
| Page fully usable | a second or so after that | about 1–2 s |

**Why min 0 is slow:** after a period with no traffic, Cloud Run shuts the app down completely. The first visitor's request has to wait while it starts back up:
1. **Starting the container, about 2–5 s.** Cloud Run has to fetch and start an image of roughly 500 MB or more, most of which is ~270–310 MB of model files and the catalog.
2. **Starting Python, about 1–2 s.** Loading numpy, scipy and FastAPI on one CPU. `--cpu-boost` helps with this step.
3. **Loading the models, probably 2–6 s.** `load_artifacts` (`src/goodrec/core/artifacts.py`) reads the model files and the reader matrix (15.7M ratings). It also rebuilds search text for all ~105k books with a SQLite query plus accent-folding. Then the homepage cover wall gets looked up by title and author.

The app doesn't answer any request until all three steps finish. That visitor sees a blank page or a spinner the whole time, and on a slow phone connection it can feel like the site is broken.

**Why min 1 is fast:** one copy of the app stays running with everything already loaded. Your README says requests take milliseconds, so page load is mostly just downloading the frontend. Cloud Run occasionally restarts that copy, but it starts the replacement before any visitor needs it.

**To get your real numbers:**
- **Logs:** the app already logs `artifacts loaded in X.Xs` at startup (`src/goodrec/api/main.py:62`). Search for it in the Cloud Run logs for `goodrec`. That covers step 3.
- **Metrics:** the Cloud Run Metrics tab has a "Container startup latency" chart that covers the whole startup.
- **Direct test:** while min-instances is still 0 and the site has sat idle for 15+ minutes, run `curl -o /dev/null -s -w '%{time_total}\n' https://<your-url>/`. Run it a second time right after for the warm comparison.

If you want to stay on min 0 for cost, there are two options. The page could show a "waking up…" message during startup. The search-text build could also be precomputed when the model files are built, which would cut a couple of seconds off step 3. I haven't made either change.

entries.text: I notice that the navigation is a little cramped on mobile. Everything along the top two toolbars is a big squished. The horizontal scroll works, but it's not as clean as would be ideal. How would you go about fixing that? I'm thinking something like a collapsable menu in the top right for the top toolbar. Maybe the lower toolbar stays horizontal scroll? I'm open to other ideas
entries.reply:
I'd do what you suggested, with a few details that make it feel finished. Here's the plan based on the current code.

**Top bar (7 buttons in `App.tsx`): collapse into a menu on phones**

At 640px wide or less, the bar would show just **📚 Shelf Life** on the left and a **☰** button on the right. Tapping ☰ drops down a full-width panel under the bar, with the 7 pages as big one-per-row items (about 44px tall, easy to tap).
- **Show the current page next to the brand**, e.g. "📚 Shelf Life · Explore". Otherwise, once the tabs are hidden, people lose track of where they are.
- **Keep the "Your books" count visible** by putting a small dot or number on the ☰ icon, so the shelf count doesn't disappear.
- **Standard menu behavior:** it closes when you pick a page, tap outside it, or press Escape. It's announced properly to screen readers, and the background page doesn't scroll while it's open.
- Desktop and tablet layouts stay exactly as they are. It's one piece of state in `App.tsx` plus a phone-only CSS rule.

Another option is a bottom tab bar, like native apps use, with Recommendations, Explore, Your books and Assistant plus a "More" item. It's easier to reach with a thumb, but there are 7 pages here, it adds another bar fixed to the screen, and it's a bigger departure from your design. I'd start with the ☰ menu.

**Lower toolbar (the Recommendations tabs): keep horizontal scroll, but polish it**

Scrolling is the right choice for tabs, because seeing them all at once matters. It just needs:
- **Scroll the selected tab into view automatically**, so a tab you picked off the right edge doesn't stay half hidden.
- **Snap to tab edges** when you let go, so it never stops with a tab cut in half.
- **Fade the edge where there's more to scroll.** The top nav already uses a fade for this (`styles.css:490`). I'd reuse it here but only show it on the side that actually has more tabs.
- Hide the scrollbar, and trim the padding a little on phones.

**Side benefit:** the top bar and the tabs both stay pinned to the top of the screen while you scroll. On a phone, those two rows take up a lot of space. A slimmer top bar gives the book list noticeably more room.

**How I'd check it:** run the app in the headless browser here and take screenshots at iPhone and small-Android widths, both before and after. I'd also run the frontend build and existing tests, then push to the branch for you to look at.

Want me to go ahead with the ☰ menu plus the tab polish?

entries.text: yeah that sounds like a good plan
entries.reply:
I've built both changes, and they're pushed to the `claude/vscode-cross-computer-access-bf9nn6` branch. Your live site doesn't change until you merge the branch and run `make deploy`. The screenshots above compare the Recommendations page on an iPhone-width screen before and after, plus one with the menu open.

**Top bar (phones only):**
- The seven links are now behind a **☰** button at the top right, which turns into an **✕** while open. The menu opens as a panel under the bar, with one big row per page and the current page highlighted.
- The bar shows which page you're on, e.g. "📚 Shelf Life · Recommendations".
- A small blue dot on ☰ stands in for the "Your books" count. The number itself still shows next to "Your books" inside the menu.
- The menu closes when you pick a page, tap outside it, or press Escape. The page behind it doesn't scroll while it's open.
- The bar is slightly shorter on phones (52px instead of 58px), which gives the book list more room.
- Desktop looks exactly as before.

**Recommendations tabs:**
- Still scroll sideways, but the selected tab now scrolls into view on its own. Your "before" screenshot shows the problem: "From your to-read" was selected but off-screen.
- The tabs snap to tab edges when you let go, the scrollbar is hidden, and a fade appears only on the edge that has more tabs.

**One extra fix:** the "Sort by / View" row was getting cut off on phones ("Predict…", "M…"). It now wraps onto two lines.

**How I tested it:**
- The frontend build passed, including TypeScript. The frontend has no automated tests.
- I ran the site in a headless browser at 390px and 360px phone widths and at desktop width, with fake data in place of the real server. There's no sideways page overflow at any width.
- In that browser I checked that Escape and picking a page both close the menu.
- I haven't tried it on a real phone. It's worth a quick tap-through after you deploy.

entries.text: can I test the new experience from my computer?
entries.reply:
Yes. Run it locally on the computer where you normally work on Shelf Life. It needs the `artifacts/` folder, which isn't in git, so use the machine you last ran `make deploy` from.

**1. Get the branch.** In the VS Code terminal:
```
git fetch origin
git checkout claude/vscode-cross-computer-access-bf9nn6
cd "01 - Shelf Life (Goodreads Recommender v2)"
```

**2. Start the app.** Use two terminals, both in that folder:
```
make serve     # API on :8000
make dev       # frontend on http://localhost:5173
```
If `make dev` complains about missing packages, run `cd frontend && npm install` first.

**3. See the phone layout in your desktop browser.** Open http://localhost:5173 in Chrome, press **Cmd+Option+I** (Mac) or **Ctrl+Shift+I** (Windows), then click the phone/tablet icon at the top left of DevTools, or press **Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+M**. Pick "iPhone 14" or similar from the device list. The ☰ menu appears at any width of 640px or less.

To try it with real data, click "See a demo" on the homepage, then go to Recommendations. You'll see the tabs scrolling sideways, and the "Sort by / View" row wrapping.

**Optional: try it on your actual phone.** A real phone is the best test for tapping and scrolling.
- **Same Wi-Fi:** run `cd frontend && npx vite --host` instead of `make dev`. It prints a "Network" address like `http://192.168.x.x:5173`; open that on your phone.
- **Private preview on Cloud Run:** this deploys the branch as a separate URL that gets no public traffic, so shelflife visitors keep seeing the current version:
  ```
  python3 scripts/code_links.py
  gcloud builds submit --project v2-book-recommender --region us-central1 --tag us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/v2-book-recommender/goodrec/app .
  gcloud run deploy goodrec --project v2-book-recommender --region us-central1 \
    --image us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/v2-book-recommender/goodrec/app --no-traffic --tag preview
  ```
  The output includes a URL starting with `https://preview---goodrec-…`. When you're happy with it, merge the branch and run `make deploy` as usual.

When you merge, the branch also brings the `--min-instances 1` Makefile change from earlier. The next real `make deploy` will apply that setting too.

There was nothing new to push: both changes were already committed to the feature branch `claude/vscode-cross-computer-access-bf9nn6` on GitHub, and nothing is left uncommitted. The branch is 2 commits ahead of `main`:

You can review and merge it here: https://github.com/mraottth/projects/compare/main...claude/vscode-cross-computer-access-bf9nn6

If you only want one of the two changes, tell me which and I'll split them into separate branches.

entries.text: great I went ahead and merged. Can you deploy?
entries.reply:
I can't deploy from here, for two reasons:
- **No Google Cloud access.** This cloud session has no `gcloud` and no credentials for your project.
- **The deploy needs your model files.** The ~300 MB `artifacts/` folder isn't in git, and `make deploy` builds it into the app image. Even with access, I'd have nothing to build.

Run it from the computer you usually deploy from:
```
git checkout main
git pull
cd "01 - Shelf Life (Goodreads Recommender v2)"
make deploy
```

That single command ships both merged changes:
- the new phone menu and tab scrolling
- `--min-instances 1`, so one copy of the app stays running and first visitors skip the slow startup

After it finishes, open the site on your phone and try the ☰ menu. To confirm the always-on setting took, open the goodrec service in Google Cloud Console → Cloud Run → Revisions and look for "Min instances: 1".

entries.text: got it - I can deploy from GCP on web, right?
entries.reply:
Partly. The Cloud Console in your browser can deploy an app image that's already built, but it can't build a new one. The phone-menu changes need a new build, and `make deploy` normally copies the ~300 MB `artifacts/` folder from your computer into it. Cloud Shell doesn't have that folder.

This merge only changed the frontend, though, so there's a workaround: in Cloud Shell, take the app image that's already running (it already contains the model files) and swap in the new frontend.

**1.** Open Cloud Shell (the `>_` icon at the top right of console.cloud.google.com), then get the code:
```
gcloud config set project v2-book-recommender
git clone https://github.com/mraottth/projects.git
cd "projects/01 - Shelf Life (Goodreads Recommender v2)"
```
If the repo is private, `git clone` will ask you to sign in. Use a GitHub personal access token as the password.

**2.** Build a new image from the current one with only the frontend replaced:
```
IMG=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/v2-book-recommender/goodrec/app
cat > Dockerfile.ui <<'EOF'
FROM node:22-slim AS frontend
WORKDIR /frontend
COPY frontend/package.json frontend/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY frontend/ ./
RUN npm run build

FROM us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/v2-book-recommender/goodrec/app:latest
RUN rm -rf /app/frontend/dist
COPY --from=frontend /frontend/dist /app/frontend/dist
EOF
gcloud auth configure-docker us-central1-docker.pkg.dev --quiet
docker build -f Dockerfile.ui -t $IMG:mobile-nav . && docker push $IMG:mobile-nav
```

**3.** Deploy it and turn on the always-on instance:
```
gcloud run deploy goodrec --region us-central1 --image $IMG:mobile-nav --min-instances 1
```
This only changes the image and min-instances. Your other Cloud Run settings stay as they are, including memory, CPU and the Assistant's API key.

**If you only want the min-instances change,** you can do that without Cloud Shell: in the console, go to Cloud Run → goodrec → **Edit & deploy new revision**, set **Minimum number of instances** to 1, and click Deploy.

I haven't run these steps myself, since I have no access to your Google Cloud project. The workaround only works when a change is purely frontend. When the Python or the models change, deploy with `make deploy` from your computer.

entries.text: let's make 3 changes on a new branch. First, let's get a little more spacing between the books as they move across the screen. As it is, they bunch up a bit too much causing distracting overlap. Second, let's add a mouseover tooltip on the options in the top toolbar (e.g. recommendations, assistant, your books, etc.). Just a couple words about what the user can do on each page. Finally, let's take a little bit of the technical detail out of the 'About' page. It should focus most on what models were used, the reasons, why, how they generally work, and the basic results.
entries.reply:
All three changes are done and pushed to a new branch, `br-flow-tooltips-about`, ready for you to review and merge: https://github.com/mraottth/projects/compare/main...br-flow-tooltips-about

**1. More space in the cover animation**

The covers bunched up for three reasons:
- They slowed almost to a stop mid-screen and piled up there.
- Covers launched back to back used neighboring rows, even though each cover is taller than the gap between rows.
- The second wave (your recommendations) started while the first was still crossing.

Now the covers move at a steady speed, alternate between rows that are far apart, and the second wave follows the first. On narrow screens fewer covers fly, rather than cramming the same number in. I measured it by playing the demo animation in a test browser:

| Desktop, 1440×900 | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Covers on screen at once | ~24 | ~17 |
| Covers more than 25% hidden behind another | 78% | 10% |

It still looks busy, just not stacked. If you want it roomier, one number controls this (`MIN_GAP` in `CoverFlow.tsx`). Setting it to 0.9 gives about 13 covers on screen with almost no overlap.

**2. Tooltips on the top menu**

On desktop, hovering over a page name (or tabbing to it) shows a short description after a brief pause. On phones there's no hover, so the same text appears as a small line under each item in the ☰ menu.

| Page | Tooltip |
|---|---|
| Recommendations | Your personal picks, with filters and a map |
| Explore | Browse and filter the whole library |
| Your books | Your shelf and reading stats |
| Assistant | Ask Claude what to read next |
| Rate books | Star books you've read to get started |
| Import | Bring in your Goodreads library |
| About | How the recommendations work |

**3. About page**

I rewrote the visible text around what each model is, why it's used, how it works in plain terms, and what the results mean:
- Each model now has a small label naming its type (for example "Matrix factorization (ALS)") and a **Why:** line.
- Jargon like "implicit ALS" and "64-dimensional taste space" is gone from the main text.
- The long paragraph on how the models are combined is now four short plain rules.
- Under the results table there are three takeaways: combining the models wins, it learns quickly, and predicted ratings are close.

While checking the takeaways against your results table, I corrected two that overstated it. At 1 rating the combined model only ties the taste model, and the improvement from 3 to 10 ratings is 1.6×, not double.

I kept the collapsed "Show technical details" sections, which hold the math and code links, and merged two that were stacked under the results. If you'd rather cut those down too, tell me which to trim.

I also updated the cover-animation notes in `CLAUDE.md`.

The frontend build passes. I checked everything in a test browser with placeholder data, at phone and desktop widths. I haven't seen it with real book covers or on a real phone.

entries.text: For the tooltip language let's change Recommendations to "See your personal picks". For Assistant it can say "Chat with AI about books and your recommendations ". For Rate book say "Rate books for better recommendations".

entries.reply:
I've sent three recordings of the "See a demo" transition, each about 10 seconds:

entries.text: Okay I actually like the before version a lot better. The issue is just that they all bunch up right in the middle (which is by design). Let's revert that animation to how it was before and then add a little randomness about where on the screen each book takes its little pause. Please share a screen recording after you make the change
entries.reply:
The animation is back to the original. Each book still eases in, pauses and speeds off, but now pauses at its own spot somewhere between about 18% and 74% of the way across the screen instead of all at the exact center. The change is pushed to `br-flow-tooltips-about`. I've sent two recordings above, one on desktop and one at phone width.

I measured it in a test browser on a 1440×900 screen with placeholder covers (this network blocks real cover images):

| | Original | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Covers in the middle fifth of the screen, on average | 26% | 15% |
| Most covers in the middle fifth at once | 26 | 16 |

The number of covers and all the timing are the same as the original. Covers will still overlap in places, because the same number are on screen, but they no longer stack up in one column in the middle.

I can't play videos here, only view still images. I confirmed the recordings finished and checked still frames from the same run, but let me know if a file doesn't play.

If you want the pause spots spread wider or kept closer to the center, it's one line in `CoverFlow.tsx` (`"--mid": ${18 + rand(i, 7) * 56}vw`). For example, `12 + … * 66` spreads them further, and `28 + … * 36` keeps them nearer the middle.

entries.text: wonderful! let's also reduce the amount of time the message is on the screen before the books enter on the Demo option from 1s to 0.75s. Once you do that you can commit, push, and merge. Then can you give me the instructions on deploying via GCP terminal?
entries.reply:
Since the last version on `main` before today's work, only the frontend, the Makefile and the docs have changed; no Python or model files. That means Cloud Shell can reuse the model files already inside your live app image and just swap in the new frontend. You don't need to upload the ~300 MB `artifacts/` folder.

## Deploy from the GCP web terminal (Cloud Shell)

**1. Open Cloud Shell.** Go to console.cloud.google.com, make sure project **v2-book-recommender** is selected, and click the **`>_`** icon at the top right. Then run:
```
gcloud config set project v2-book-recommender
```

**2. Get the latest code.**
```
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/mraottth/projects.git 2>/dev/null || (cd projects && git checkout main && git pull)
cd ~/projects/"01 - Shelf Life (Goodreads Recommender v2)"
git log --oneline -1
```
The last line should say `Merge pull request #8 …`. If the repo is private, `git clone` asks for a username and password: use your GitHub username and a personal access token (github.com → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens) as the password.

**3. Refresh the About page's code links.**
```
python3 scripts/code_links.py
```

**4. Build a new image: the current live image with the new frontend swapped in.**
```
IMG=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/v2-book-recommender/goodrec/app
LIVE=$(gcloud run services describe goodrec --region us-central1 --format='value(spec.template.spec.containers[0].image)')
echo "Live image: $LIVE"

cat > Dockerfile.ui <<EOF
FROM node:22-slim AS frontend
WORKDIR /frontend
COPY frontend/package.json frontend/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY frontend/ ./
RUN npm run build

FROM $LIVE
RUN rm -rf /app/frontend/dist
COPY --from=frontend /frontend/dist /app/frontend/dist
EOF

gcloud auth configure-docker us-central1-docker.pkg.dev --quiet
docker build -f Dockerfile.ui -t $IMG:ui-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) .
docker push $IMG:ui-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
```
This bases the new image on whatever is running right now, so the models and server code stay exactly as they are.

**5. Deploy.**
```
gcloud run deploy goodrec --region us-central1 \
  --image $IMG:ui-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) --min-instances 1
```
Only the image and min-instances change. Memory, CPU and the Assistant's API key carry over from the current setup. When it finishes, it prints the service URL.

**6. Check the live site.**
- **See a demo:** the caption shows briefly, then covers fly in and pause at different spots.
- **Tooltips:** hover over the top menu items on desktop.
- **Phone menu:** open ☰ on your phone and check for the one-line descriptions.
- **About:** the page has the new, plainer text.

**If something looks wrong,** go to Cloud Run → goodrec → **Revisions**, pick the previous revision, and choose **Manage traffic** to send 100% back to it. That rolls back instantly.

**Two caveats:**
- I haven't run these steps myself, because I have no access to your Google Cloud project. If a step errors, paste the output here.
- This shortcut only works for frontend-only changes. For anything that touches the Python code or the models, use `make deploy` from your own computer.

entries.text: can you come up with 3 other names instead of shelf life? I do like it, but I want to see if there are other good options
entries.reply:
Here are three alternatives, each playing up a different side of the app:

1. **Next Chapter.** Says plainly what the site does: it helps you find what to read next. It's warm, obvious and easy to remember. The catch is that it's a common phrase, so a distinctive web address or search ranking will be harder to get.

2. **Kindred Reads.** Built around the "readers like you" idea, which is the heart of how the recommendations work: people with your taste loved these. It fits naturally next to the Popular and Top rated tabs.

3. **Dog-Ear.** Short and bookish, named after folding a page corner to mark something worth coming back to. It has the same playful tone as Shelf Life and would make a nice logo.

I'd still keep **Shelf Life**. It's clever, it hints at your reading history (your shelf, over time), and it's already woven through the site and repo.

I haven't checked domains or whether other products already use these names; that's worth doing before you commit. If you want to switch, renaming is quick: the name appears in the header, the About page and the docs.

entries.text: I noticed that the best match recommendations have some very low predicted scores. I know we fixed that on the For You page. Would implementing the same fix be a frontend only change? Would deployment be different than the last few changes?
entries.reply:
No, it wouldn't be frontend-only.

**Why you're seeing it.** The fix we made for For you is a filter in the Python ranking code (`prediction_floor()` in `src/goodrec/core/scoring.py`). It drops any book predicted below your average rating minus 0.25 stars. It only runs for the For you tab:
- **Popular and Top rated** ("…with readers like you") skip it on purpose. There's a comment in `src/goodrec/api/main.py` that says "readers tabs: no floor". Those lists show what similar readers read or loved, even when the rating model expects you'd like a book less.
- **From your to-read** isn't filtered either.
- **With fewer than 5 ratings,** the filter is off everywhere, including For you.

So if you saw low predictions under Best match on Popular or Top rated, that's the gap. It would be about a 10-line change in the Python server (`main.py`, where those two lists are built), plus updating the About page line that says those lists aren't floored.

**Deployment would be slightly different.** The Cloud Shell steps I gave you only replace the frontend, so a server change wouldn't go live. You have two options:
1. **`make deploy` from your computer.** This is the standard route.
2. **Cloud Shell, with one extra line.** No model files or packages would change, so the same trick still works: add `COPY src/ /app/src/` and `COPY config/ /app/config/` to that little Dockerfile so the new server code goes in along with the new frontend. Everything else stays the same.

Before I build it, two quick questions:
- **Which tab were you on?** If it was For you itself, something else is going on, and I'd want to look at that first.
- **Do you want the filter on both Popular and Top rated?** Filtering those lists changes their meaning a bit: they'd become "books readers like you loved *and* we think you'd like." Would you also want it on From your to-read? I'd leave to-read alone, since you chose those books yourself.

entries.text:
[screenshot]

I guess I'm confused why these are the top 2 Best Matches in the Popular with Readers Like You section. It looks like they're not that popular with readers like me. Other books have higher "% similar readers read it" and higher average scores among similar readers
entries.reply:
The ranking is doing what it was designed to do, but that design doesn't match what the tab name promises.

**How "Popular with readers like you" ranks books.** Best match on this tab doesn't use predicted rating or the "Readers like you" average at all. It uses one score:

> share of your 300 most similar readers who read the book ÷ √(share of *all* readers who read it)

The division exists so universal bestsellers like Harry Potter don't fill the list. But it rewards books that are rare overall much more than books that are common among readers like you. With rough numbers:
- **Superintelligence:** read by 5% of your similar readers but only a tiny slice of all readers (about 6k Goodreads ratings). Dividing by a very small number makes a big score, so it lands at #1.
- **A book 30% of your similar readers read,** but which is also widely read everywhere, gets divided by a much bigger number and falls below it.

So the list really shows **books unusually over-represented among readers like you**, not the books most popular with them. That's why a book with 5% reach and a 2.56 prediction can top it, which is a bad #1 by any reasonable standard.

**How I'd fix it.** Everything below is in the Python server, not the frontend.
1. **Require real reach.** Only rank books read by at least ~10% of your similar readers (the exact cutoff is a setting). This alone would drop Superintelligence from the top.
2. **Soften the bestseller penalty.** Change the square root to a gentler power (`pop_damping` in `config/pipeline.yaml`, 0.5 → about 0.25). Very common books still get pushed down a little, but reach matters more.
3. **Apply the For you floor here too.** Hide books predicted well below your average, so a 2.56 never shows up for someone who rates around 4.

I'd do all three, with 1 and 2 as adjustable settings. I can't try out the cutoffs here, because the model files aren't in this cloud session. So I'd pick sensible defaults, and you'd sanity-check them locally (`make serve` + `make dev`) with your own library before deploying.

**On deployment:** this touches the server and a config file, so use `make deploy` from your computer. Or, in Cloud Shell, add two lines to the little Dockerfile so the new code and settings go in with the frontend:
```
COPY src/ /app/src/
COPY config/ /app/config/
```

Top rated has a similar issue. It ranks purely by similar readers' average rating, so a book 5 of them rated 5★ can outrank one 40 of them rated 4.6★. Want me to make these changes to Popular, and also give Top rated the floor and a higher minimum number of raters?
